entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen29713" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29714" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29715" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29715" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29714" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29716" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins with setting forth the very strong bias which the people of Judah had to idolatry, with the fatal consequences, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.1-Jer.17.4">Jer 17:1-4</reference>. The happiness of the man that trusted in Jehovah is then beautifully contrasted with the opposite character, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.5-Jer.17.8">Jer 17:5-8</reference>. God alone knows the deceitfulness and wretchedness of the heart of man, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.9">Jer 17:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.10">Jer 17:10</reference>. The comparison of a bird's hatching the eggs of another of a different species, which will soon forsake her, is highly expressive of the vanity of ill-acquired riches, which often disappoint the owner, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.11">Jer 17:11</reference>. The prophet continues the same subject in his own person, appeals to God for his sincerity, and prays that the evil intended him by his enemies may revert on their own heads, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.12-Jer.17.18">Jer 17:12-18</reference>. The remaining part of the chapter is a distinct prophecy relating to the due observance of the Sabbath, enforced both by promises and threatenings, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.19-Jer.17.27">Jer 17:19-27</reference>. <div eID="gen29716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29717" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29718" type="x-p"/> The sin of Judah - Idolatry. <div eID="gen29718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29719" type="x-p"/> Is written with a pen of iron - It is deeply and indelibly written in their heart, and shall be as indelibly written in their punishment. Writing with the point of a diamond must refer to glass, or some vitrified substance, as it is distinguished here from engraving with a steel burine, or graver. Their altars show what the deities are which they worship. There may be reference here to the different methods of recording events in those days: - <div eID="gen29719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29720" type="x-p"/> 1. A pen or stile of iron, for engraving on lead or wood. <div eID="gen29720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29721" type="x-p"/> 2. A point of a diamond, for writing on vitreous substances. <div eID="gen29721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29722" type="x-p"/> 3. Writing on tables of brass or copper. <div eID="gen29722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29723" type="x-p"/> 4. Writing on the horns of the altars the names of the deities worshipped there. This is probable. <div eID="gen29723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29724" type="x-p"/> In several parts of India, and all through Ceylon, an iron or steel pen is used universally; with these the natives form the letters by incisions on the outer rind of the palm leaf. Books written in this way are very durable. This pen is broad at the top, has a very fine sharp point, and is sharp at one side as a knife, to shave and prepare the palm leaf. A pen of this description now lies before me.
entries.content_plain: Introduction This chapter begins with setting forth the very strong bias which the people of Judah had to idolatry, with the fatal consequences, Jer 17:1-4 . The happiness of the man that trusted in Jehovah is then beautifully contrasted with the opposite character, Jer 17:5-8 . God alone knows the deceitfulness and wretchedness of the heart of man, Jer 17:9 , Jer 17:10 . The comparison of a bird's hatching the eggs of another of a different species, which will soon forsake her, is highly expressive of the vanity of ill-acquired riches, which often disappoint the owner, Jer 17:11 . The prophet continues the same subject in his own person, appeals to God for his sincerity, and prays that the evil intended him by his enemies may revert on their own heads, Jer 17:12-18 . The remaining part of the chapter is a distinct prophecy relating to the due observance of the Sabbath, enforced both by promises and threatenings, Jer 17:19-27 . Verse 1 The sin of Judah - Idolatry. Is written with a pen of iron - It is deeply and indelibly written in their heart, and shall be as indelibly written in their punishment. Writing with the point of a diamond must refer to glass, or some vitrified substance, as it is distinguished here from engraving with a steel burine, or graver. Their altars show what the deities are which they worship. There may be reference here to the different methods of recording events in those days: - 1. A pen or stile of iron, for engraving on lead or wood. 2. A point of a diamond, for writing on vitreous substances. 3. Writing on tables of brass or copper. 4. Writing on the horns of the altars the names of the deities worshipped there. This is probable. In several parts of India, and all through Ceylon, an iron or steel pen is used universally; with these the natives form the letters by incisions on the outer rind of the palm leaf. Books written in this way are very durable. This pen is broad at the top, has a very fine sharp point, and is sharp at one side as a knife, to shave and prepare the palm leaf. A pen of this description now lies before me.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen29725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29726" type="x-p"/> O my mountain in the field - The prophet here addresses the land of Judea, which was a mountainous country, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.25">Deu 3:25</reference>; but Jerusalem itself may be meant, which is partly built upon hills which, like itself, are elevated above the rest of the country.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen29726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29727" type="x-p"/> Cursed be the man that trusteth in man - This reprehends their vain confidence in trusting in Egypt, which was too feeble itself to help, and, had it been otherwise, too ill disposed towards them to help them heartily. An arm of flesh is put here for a weak and ineffectual support. And he who, in reference to the salvation of his soul, trusts in an arm of flesh - in himself or others, or in any thing he has done or suffered, will inherit a curse instead of a blessing.

It shall be strong and vigorous, its leaf always green; and shall produce plenty of fruit in its season.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen29732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29733" type="x-p"/> The heart is deceitful - עקב הלב akob halleb, "the heart is supplanting - tortuous - full of windings - insidious;" lying ever at the catch; striving to avail itself of every favorable circumstance to gratify its propensities to pride, ambition, evil desire, and corruption of all kinds. <div eID="gen29733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29734" type="x-p"/> And desperately wicked - ואנש הוא veanush hu, and is wretched, or feeble; distressed beyond all things, in consequence of the wickedness that is in it. I am quite of Mr. Parkhurst's opinion, that this word is here badly translated as אנש anash is never used in Scripture to denote wickedness of any kind. My old MS. Bible translates thus: - Schrewid is the herte of a man: and unserchable: who schal knowen it? <div eID="gen29734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29735" type="x-p"/> Who can know it? - It even hides itself from itself; so that its owner does not know it. A corrupt heart is the worst enemy the fallen creature can have; it is full of evil devices, - of deceit, of folly, and abomination, and its owner knows not what is in him till it boils over, and is often past remedy before the evil is perceived. Therefore trust not in man whose purposes are continually changing, and who is actuated only by motives of self-interest.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen29735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29736" type="x-p"/> I the Lord search the heart - The Lord is called by his apostles, <reference osisRef="Act.1.24">Act 1:24</reference>, Καρδιογνωστης, the Knower of the heart. To him alone can this epithet be applied; and it is from him alone that we can derive that instruction by which we can in any measure know ourselves.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen29736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29737" type="x-p"/> As the partridge - קרא kore. It is very likely that this was a bird different from our partridge. The text Dr. Blayney translates thus: - (As) the kore that hatcheth what it doth not lay (So is) he who getteth riches, and not according to right. "The covetous man," says Dahler, "who heaps up riches by unjust ways, is compared to a bird which hatches the eggs of other fowls. And as the young, when hatched, and able at all to shift for themselves, abandon her who is not their mother, and leave her nothing to compensate her trouble, so the covetous man loses those unjustly-gotten treasures, and the fruit of his labor." <div eID="gen29737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29738" type="x-p"/> And at his end shall be a fool - Shall be reputed as such. He was a fool all the way through; he lost his soul to get wealth, and this wealth he never enjoyed. To him also are applicable those strong words of the poet: - "O cursed lust of gold! when for thy sake <div eID="gen29738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29739" type="x-p"/> The wretch throws up his interest in both worlds. <div eID="gen29739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29740" type="x-p"/> First starved in this, then damned in that to come." <div eID="gen29740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29741" type="x-p"/> Blair.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen29746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29747" type="x-p"/> I have not hastened from being a pastor - Dr. Blayney translates thus: "But I have not been in haste to outrun thy guidance." I was obliged to utter thy prediction; but I have not hastened the evil day. For the credit of my prophecy I have not desired the calamity to come speedily; I have rather pleaded for respite. I have followed thy steps, and proclaimed thy truth. I did not desire to be a prophet; but thou hast commanded, and I obeyed.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen29751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29752" type="x-p"/> Take heed to yourselves and bear no burden - From this and the following verses we find the ruin of the Jews attributed to the breach of the Sabbath; as this led to a neglect of sacrifice, the ordinances of religion, and all public worship, so it necessarily brought with it all immorality. This breach of the Sabbath was that which let in upon them all the waters of God's wrath.

navigation_sections.title: Introduction
navigation_sections.content_plain: Introduction This chapter begins with setting forth the very strong bias which the people of Judah had to idolatry, with the fatal consequences, Jer 17:1-4 . The happiness of the man that trusted in Jehovah is then beautifully contrasted with the opposite character, Jer 17:5-8 . God alone knows the deceitfulness and wretchedness of the heart of man, Jer 17:9 , Jer 17:10 . The comparison of a bird's hatching the eggs of another of a different species, which will soon forsake her, is highly expressive of the vanity of ill-acquired riches, which often disappoint the owner, Jer 17:11 . The prophet continues the same subject in his own person, appeals to God for his sincerity, and prays that the evil intended him by his enemies may revert on their own heads, Jer 17:12-18 . The remaining part of the chapter is a distinct prophecy relating to the due observance of the Sabbath, enforced both by promises and threatenings, Jer 17:19-27 .
